FOUR COMPONENTS OF LIFE 

“REASON faces up to life, and sees things as they are. 
HOPE sees things as they ought to be and wishes on a star. 

FAITH dreams of miracles to come, that only God can 
do. 

LOVE goes to work with patient hands to make these 
dreams come true. 

SPECIAL 

by Arlena MacDonald and Teri Fernandez 

“Special” is a word used to describe something one-of-a- 
kind, like you or a sunset, or a person who spreads love with a 
smile or a kind gesture. 

“Special” describes people who act from the heart and who 
keep in mind the heart of others. 

“Special” is the word which best describes a hug. But when 
you hug me, please don’t try to straighten out the bands or 
hammer down the kinks or smooth the rough edges. 

Just put your arms around the whole of me. 

The weak and tough spots. 

The flaws and fears 
And make it as special as it can be. 

HELEN KELLER 

“Use your eyes,” wrote HELEN KELLER, “as if tomorrow 
you would be stricken blind; hear the music of voices, the 
song of a bird, as if you would be stricken deaf tomorrow. 
Touch each object as if tomorrow your tactile sense would 
fail. Smell the perfume of flowers, taste with relish each mor¬ 
sel, as if tomorrow you could never smell and taste again.”

DESIDERATA (Revised) 

Go placidly amid the noise and excitement of summer 
camping, 

And remember that this is one sign of good camping. 

As far as possible without surrender 

Be on good terms with all your fellow leaders. 

Plan your programmes carefully and cheerfully; 

And listen to others, 

Even the youngest camper; 

He/she will give you many moments of joy. 

Avoid loud and aggressive gatherings of leaders. 

Except when you are part of one. 

If you compare your campers with others, 

Do not become vain or bitter; 

For success can only be judged by the smiles on their 
faces. 

Enjoy your achievements as well as your plans. 

Keep in mind the aims of camping, 

However hard to understand at times, 

It is a real possession in the changing fortunes of time. 
Exercise caution with the camp funds; 

For parents work hard for this fee. 

But let this not blind you to what camping is all about... 
Be yourself. 

Especially, have fun. 

Neither “bum out” too soon; 

For in the face of all aridity and disenchantment 
Those campers are depending on you. 

Take kindly the counsel of your director, 

He will help you all that he can. 

Nurture strength of spirit in case of a failure, 

But do not blame yourself... you have done your best. 
And what you think of as “failure” may be “super fun” to your 
campers. 

Beyond a wholesome discipline, 

Be gentle with yourself. 

You are the most important person in Camping; 

We need more leaders like yourself 
To help the youth of this world. 

And whether or not it is clear to you. 

You are molding the future of this country. 

Therefore, be at peace with God, 

Whatever you conceive Him to be. 

And whatever your labours and aspirations 
In the noisy confusion of summer camping. 

Keep peace with yourself. 

With all its hard work and sometimes frustration, 

It is a wonderful experience. 

Be cheerful... strive for good Camping... 

(from the Sherbrooke Lake Camp Leaders' Handbook) 
(found in United Church Camping - Spring 1985)

WHAT’S IN sssk UN NOM .. . 

A NAME? WMM^ SON HISTOIRE 


CAMP HE HO HA (he ho ha) 

The name stands for: HEaltli HOpe HAppiness 

In 1959 Walter Bates, Bob Sewell and Dr. Ken Gordon, mem¬ 
bers of the South Edmonton Kiwanis Club, approached the then 
Minister of Health about the need for camping facilities for the 
handicapped. It was approved in principle and before long a site 
on a peninsula on Lake Isle was drawn up. 

The Alberta Camp Council was formed with representation 
from five organizations involved in work with the handicapped. 
These were the South Edmonton Kiwanis Club; Canadian 


PHILOSOPHY 

Everyone has the right to recreation (if desired) regardless ol 
their disability and therefore, should be encouraged to reach 
his/her potential. Camp He Ho Ha provides an outdoor rec¬ 
reational experience for those who require or desire special 
facilities. 

The Camp's facility and program is set up to serve as many 
individual needs as possible. Hopefully it will enhance 
everyone's spirit of adventure, providing an incentive 
throughout the summer. 



Indoor Pool - Camp He Ho Ha 


Diabetic Association; The Edmonton Cerebral Palsy Associa¬ 
tion and the Associated Canadian Travellers (Edmonton Club) 
who administer the Northern Alberta Crippled Children's 
Fu nd. 

The above organization contributed funds in varying 
amounts to get the project started and with the donation of 
buildings from Imperial Oil Limited, plus the construction of a 
medical centre by Mr. & Mrs. Muttart, the Camp was in opera¬ 
tion in 1960. 

In 1963, the Associated Canadian Travellers built a heated 
swimming pool, and it was soon evident that the temporary 
facilities had to be replaced. Construction of large wood frame 
cabins commenced in 1966. with the Associated Canadian 
Travellers underwriting the costs of construction. 

I n 1969. the A.C.T. drew up an operating lease with the Alberta 
Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled (ARCD). which had. 
several years earlier, assumed ownership of the facilities from 
the original Alberta Camp Council. The reasoning behind this 
was that a similar camp had to be built in the southern halfof the 
province and the Easter Seal Ability Council, (formerly the 
ARCD). was the logical provincial body for assuming province 
wide responsibility through their Easter Seal franchise. 

However, by 1969 it was evident that Easter Seal Funds were 
inadequate to operate and maintain both camps and the A.C.I. 
assumed operational responsibility of Camp He Ho Ha such 
that the Northern Alberta Crippled Children's Fund would 
guarantee the deficit incurred by the camp. 

By 1980. Camp He Ho Ha was offering6 programs for various 
age and disability groups. The 8()'s proved to be a decade of 
change. Within 4 years the camp jumped from serving 500 dis¬ 
abled individuals to approximately 1.000 in a year by increasing 
both the number of camps offered and the capacity of each 
camp. Opportunities for year round use on an independent 
basis became a reality as a result of a massive rebuilding 
ca mpaign. 


Arts & Crafts and Administration Centre 

Camp He Ho Ha 


OVERALL PRINCIPLES 


In your efforts to incorporate these needs, don't losesightofan 
over-riding principle that learning should be fun. It is your res¬ 
ponsibility to use leadership techniques that will incorporate 
fun as well as motivate campers to participate. 

In all activities staff should place “Campers First" which does 
not mean that you do things for them but rather that their needs 
are put before your own. We all like to be needed and help others 
but “Campers First" means that we look at the camper's needs 
first — can they do it on their own. If the answer is yes. then let 
them — your impatience, your need to win, your need to help is 
secondary. Look at the ability NOT the disability and do all you 
can to create an opportunity for independence and skill 
development always remembering to treat everyone as an

PROGRAMMES SUR LE MILIEU 


CERAMIC WHISTLE 

Fanciful creatures with voices. 

Materials: 

Small package of self-hardening Mexican pottery clay 
Wax paper 

Rolling pin, dowel or tube for rolling clay 
Knife 

Medium size ball (tennis or golf) 

Pencil 

To Make 

1. Take a ball of clay about 2” in diameter, and place on a 
piece of wax paper. Roll with the rolling pin to about 1/4” 
thickness. 

2. Cover the golf or tennis ball with wax paper. We used clear 
plastic tape to hold the waxpaper in place. 

3. Place the ball on the clay. Wrap the clay around the ball 
completely. Work with the clay until it is smooth and 
round. 

4. Place the clay-covered ball in the sun or near a heater until 
partially dry. 

5. With the knife, cut the clay — not the ball — in half (A). 
Remove the plastic-wrapped ball from the center. 

6. Place the two clay halves back together, making a sphere 
(B). Take more clay and carefully fill the knife edge. Using 
water to thin the clay makes it more workable. 

7. Take another piece of clay — about a T’ball — and make a 
round, long shape, 2” long and 1/2” in diameter (C). This is 
for the mouthpiece. 

8. With a knife, make a flat hole through the center, down the 
length of the clay mouthpiece (D). This is to blow through. 

9. Cut a hole in the clay ball, about 1 /2” in diameter. With the 
knife, bevel the edge around this hole (E). 

10. Attach mouthpiece to the edge of this hole, by adding a 
little clay and water. Smooth edges, making sure not to 
squeeze the mouthpiece so that the air won’t flow through it. 
The air should go through the mouthpiece and hit the 1/2” air 
hole in the bottom of the ball —just passing over it, like blow¬ 
ing across the top of the jug (F). Adjust mouthpiece for proper 
angle to make sound. 

11. Make ahole in the side of the ball about 1/4” in diameter 
(G). At this point, you may add a head, a tail or, with the pen¬ 
cil, make race designs in the clay while it is still workable. 
When you have achieved your fanciful design, place the 
whistle in the sun or near a heater to dry. 


SPRING WILLOW WHISTLE 


SPRING WILLOW WHISTLE 

This whistle is most easily made in the spring when the run¬ 
ning sap makes the willow bark slip off easily. It is a favourite 
old-fashioned toy. 

Materials: 

4” to 6” piece of willow, about 5/8” in diameter 
Pocket knife 

To Make 

1. Cut the piece of willow about 4” long, making sure it is 
straight. 

2. Make a small notch about 1/4” deep 1/2” from one end. 
Starting about 1” from end, according to size of branch, cut 
branch on a slant to first cut. Taper blowing end (A). 

3. Using handle of knife, tap center of branch gently until the 
bark slips off in an unbroken tube (B). Dipping in water 
may help. 

4. On the inner piece of wood, cut a long notch to within 1/2” 
of the straight end. Cut a thin strip off the blowing end for an 
air passage (C). 

5. Slide bark back and line up the notches. 

6. Test by blowing; if the tone is poor, make the air strip 
wider. 


CERAMIC WHISTLE 







29 








SHEPHERD’S PIPE (Recorder Type) 

The gentle sound of this instrument entertained the shep¬ 
herd and kept the sheep from wandering too far around the 
mountain. It is important to remember that the tone of the 
instrument comes from directing a strong stream of air 
against a sharp surface. Study the illustrations carefully and 
use a sharp knife on the airhole! 

Materials 

Bamboo, 12” long and with at least a 5/8” drill and 3/16” bit 
inside diameter, or stiff plastic tube 
Small round file or garden hose 
Sharp knife 

Cork or wood plug to fit inside the tube 

Pencil 

Coping saw 

To Make 

1. If you are using bamboo, clean and smooth the inside of 
the stalk. 

2. Measure 1” from blowing end and cut an air hole 1/2” 
square. Note the sharp, slanting cut on one side (A). 

3. Measure the cork or wood plug and cut it, if necessary to 
make sure it ends just at the air hole in the bamboo. Cut a 
slanting air passage 3/16” to 1/8” along the top edge of the 
plug (B). You may enlarge it later, but start small. 

4. Insert plug in the end of the bamboo. Make sure that the 
air will blow against the sharp edge of the airhole (C). 

5. Make the air passage a little larger if the sound is weak. 
Blow gently and keep trying -this is the hardest part. 

6. Tune pipe to lowest note by sawing off the end 1/8” at a 
time-measurements should give a C scale going up from 
middle C. 

7. To make finger holes, draw a straight line from middle 
of air hole to the far end of the pipe (D). 

8. Mark the spot for each finger hole along this line, begin¬ 
ning 2” up from the end of the pipe (E). Notice that hole bis 
played on a hole underneath the top hole, which is c, an oc¬ 
tave higher than the original note. 

9. Drill a 3/16” hole at hole c. Blow to test pitch. Raise the 
pitch by enlarging the hole slightly on the mouthpiece side. 
Lower the pitch by enlarging toward the open end. 

10. Tune each note before drilling the next one. Work 
carefully, but if you make a mistake, put some cloth tape 
across part of the hole. 

To Play 

Hold pipe with left thumb on hole b and three fingers above 
the pipe. The right hand has three fingers poised over the re¬ 
maining holes. Blow gently. Place index finger of left hand 
on hole c, thus covering two holes. Then cover remaining 
holes consecutively, until all holes are closed. You will then 
have played a scale. 

Hint 

You may wish to make the mouthpiece more comfortable 
by tapering it; make your cut starting 1/2” from the end (see 
diagram).
